ai_summary: Great Britain’s power system currently records a total wind output of 5.0 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output providing 2.6 GW, representing 25.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This localized generation highlights stark regional disparities in grid decarbonization: Scottish carbon intensity sits at a remarkably clean 5 gCO2/kWh, compared to 223 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. However, severe cross-border transmission bottlenecks continue to prevent this zero-carbon energy from reaching southern demand centers. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 11.8 GWh at a direct constraint cost of about £504,648. To balance the system and replace this lost renewable volume, fossil generation was re-dispatched downstream, resulting in an estimated 2,234,799 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and producing an additional 4,117 tonnes CO2. Annualizing today's run-rate yields an estimated total yearly cost of £184 million in curtailment expenditure. When spread across standard national annual electricity demand, these network balancing inefficiencies ultimately filter down to consumers, increasing everybody’s invoice in the UK by an estimated £0.70/MWh. Accelerating transmission reinforcement remains essential to eliminating these recurring financial and environmental penalties.
